idiom_name: class/object facade with constructor-injected services (Scala 2 and 3)
implementation_notes: The Scala facade is a class or object with a small method set over injected services - the same shape as the GoF class - and package objects were the Scala 2 way to put facade members directly into a package's scope. Scala 3 replaces that with top-level definitions and export clauses, which the language documentation names as supporting the facade design pattern: private internal objects are composed and `export Impl.*` makes exactly their members part of the public package API. Use the class when the facade has state, needs substitution, or must evolve polymorphically; use export clauses when the facade is a curated re-export of an internal composition.
pitfalls: Package objects are deprecated in Scala 3; new facades should use top-level definitions or export clauses instead.
`export` copies members rather than forwarding a type in every case: exported members are not virtual, overload and implicit-resolution subtleties apply, and you cannot override them later.
Exporting case classes or their companion members fixes internal shapes as public API; export a curated alias or trait instead.

variants.name: Top-level export-clause facade (Scala 3)
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3's export clauses were introduced precisely to keep the facade idiom that package objects enabled: private objects mix in the internal implementations, and one export clause makes their members available as the package's public API without inheritance. Prefer this form for library entry points where the facade is a curated composition rather than a stateful coordinator, and keep the internal objects private so the exported surface is the only contract.
pitfalls: Export clauses copy members, so later changes to Impl's signatures are source-visible as API changes; treat the exported set as a published contract.
Ambiguous or conflicting members from multiple exported objects surface as compile errors at the export site, which is easy to misread as an internal bug.
